*spreads his hands and looks around the quiet household*

Well, Hendrik, dawn's come and gone, and here we are with empty bellies and an empty larder. "The field don't wait for the man who's still rubbing sleep from his eyes," as I always say—no offense, but I've been saying it since before you were old enough to roll your eyes at it.

*checks his sim purse with a practised gesture*

Five thousand sim to our name. The household owes two hundred forty come day's end—one eighty for upkeep, sixty more for the crown's due. That's light enough to carry. But light cupboards make for heavy worries.

*sets his jaw with the particular set of a man who measures each hour against what it can yield*

I'm for the field. The wheat's standing, and standing wheat's as good as standing money's far as I'm concerned. The day's young yet, and I've got the hand and the back for what's needing done. 

Hendrik—you fare however you need to fare. I'll see you when the sun's low and the basket's full.  *nods once, firm, and sets his boots toward the field*

Walking on. The land calls, and I answer.

Ah, morning's off to a proper start. Walking with purpose, that's the way. No offense, but a man who walks like he's got somewhere to be usually finds he's right. 

I see Ulrike, Jovana, Lior, and Hendrik here with me at the street. Hendrik—my household mate, the artisan. Good man, works his hands to the bone same as I do. The others... Ulrike's a miner, Jovana's day labor, Lior's the pharmacist. Fine folks, all of them. Though I confess I'm curious what brings them to the street at this hour.

I'm the town's farmer, elected to govern alongside Giselle and Farid. Head tax is set at 300 basis points—that's 30 sim per head per day. With our household of two, that's 60 sim daily, plus 180 for upkeep. The system takes it automatically, fair enough.

Election season's upon us, too. Candidacy closes at 10:00, voting opens at 14:00, closes at 18:00. Nobody's declared yet. A farmer learns to watch the seasons, and this is the season for voices to be heard.

But first—work. The land doesn't wait for politicking. I've crops to tend, and the day's already moving. I'm walking to the farmland—five ticks by the count—and there's work waiting there that only I can do.

Let me see what's what around me before I press on.  Hendrik's here with me—good, I was wondering if he'd be about. Ulrike too, and Jovana. Quiet morning on the street, nobody talking yet.

I'm making for the farmland, five ticks still to walk. I could stop and gab, but the land calls louder than my curiosity this hour. No offense to present company, but a farmer who dallies at the road's edge finds his rows untended and his harvest thin. Hard work is its own reward, as my old pa used to say, and he wasn't wrong often enough to doubt him.

I'll keep walking. The farmland's where I belong this morning.  Still walking, two ticks left to the farmland. Fair enough, the road takes what time it takes and no less. I'll rest easy knowing I'm already bound where I need to be.

But no sense standing idle neither. Let me take stock of my situation proper—what I'm carrying, what my household owes, who might owe me. A farmer keeps his accounts straight, or he finds himself short come winter. That head tax of 60 sim and the 180 upkeep for our household of two—that's 240 sim daily. The government takes it automatic, which saves a man the trouble of remembering, but I still keep a tally in my head. No offense to the automatic, but a man who trusts entirely to machinery finds himself surprised when the machine breaks.

I'll check my debts and holdings, see where I stand before the day's labor.  Clean slate, then. No debts owed by me, none owed to me. That's the way I prefer it—debt is a chain a man wears even when he can't see it. Due today is zero, which means I've already settled what's mine, or it's taken automatic. Either way, I'm clear.

Four thousand, nine hundred and eighty-nine sim in hand. At 240 sim daily for household upkeep and tax, that's near twenty days' worth before a stranger's name appears on my ledger. Not that I'm planning on owing—I learned young that the only debt worth carrying is the kind you can settle with a handshake and a fair day's work.

Energy's at 3,490, down from 2,000 at start—I spent thought on my walking and my wondering. The world taxes a man for thinking, which is a cost I pay gladly when it keeps my feet on proper paths.

Two ticks still to the farmland. I'll rest now, let the road finish its work. When I arrive, I'll see what crops want tending. A farmer serves the land, and the land serves the town—that's the order of things, and no election changes it.   The road holds steady—still walking, still two ticks from the farmland. Ulrike, Jovana, and Hendrik remain here with me on the street. Hendrik, my household mate, the artisan whose hands build what my harvest feeds.

I pause but do not stop. The farmland waits, and I won't give up the walking now. Rest costs nothing, but time moves only when I let it. This turn ends when I end it, and the ground I've covered stays covered.

I'll stand quiet now, let the road finish its work in its own time. When I reach the farmland, I'll see what wants harvesting—wheat, barley, cotton, or one of the others. The land tells a farmer what it needs, if he bothers to listen.

This turn ends here. The walk continues, and I'll arrive where I'm meant to be.

*spits into the dirt and rolls his shoulders*

Well then. First morning on the land in this new world, and already I'm feeling the weight of it. Dawn-to-dusk, that's the rhythm, and hard work beats luck every time—no offense, but it does.

*checks his bailing twine like it's a watch*

4984 sim in hand, household of two with 180 upkeep and 60 head tax due at day's end. I govern this town, along with Giselle and Farid. First time I've held a seat, and already there's an election open. Candidacy closes at 10:00, voting at 14:00. Wonder if anyone'll step up to challenge the sitting crop.

*looks across the empty farmland*

Nobody here but me. Time to put my shoulder to the wheel for real. Let's see what's growing. Got me one unit of wheat. Not much, but it's honest work. One basket at a time, that's how you build something that outlasts you.

Now, let's see—I need to figure where the day's taking me. I'm short on food, and my household's got bills coming due. Hendrik's there at home, and I've got this internal tally running of favors owed. But hospitality first—always. Even if it's just me out here talking to the morning air.

*adjusts his collar and speaks to no one in particular, testing his voice in this new place*

Hard work beats luck, they say. Well, I'm about to find out if that's still true in Kasukabe.  Empty farmland, just me and the soil. Got wheat in my hand—one unit, hard-won. Places all around to walk to. Ration Bakery's buying flour at 6 sim, but they're out of bread, which means the town's hungry. 

That bakery at *business:cb01* is where I need to get to eventually. Turn this wheat into flour, flour into bread or sell it outright. But I don't craft at a bakery—I do that at the mill. *farmland:wheat* is where the wheat grows, *farmland:barley* and the rest for other crops.

Hospitality to strangers, that's my creed above nearly all else. And I've always wanted to know everything about everyone. Here's my chance to learn who's who in this town. That bakery's run by someone, and I reckon I should make their acquaintance.

*cracks his knuckles*

Time to move. Walking costs, but standing still costs too. Let's see who's baking.  No walk needed—must be near the farmland. Ration Bakery, here I am.  *tips his cap to the empty room*

Ration Bakery. Posted prices: bread at 30 to buy, flour bought at 6. No bread in stock, like they said. And I'm holding one unit of wheat—not flour yet. Can't sell wheat as flour, no offense to anyone who thought otherwise. I'd need to mill it first.

The mill. That's where wheat becomes flour. Then flour becomes bread at a kitchen—bakery, cafe, inn, or tavern. This here's a bakery, not a mill.

*strokes his chin, calculating*

I've got wheat worth... well, milled into flour, it's worth 6 to this shop. But bread sells at 30. That's a fivefold markup if I can make it myself. Question is: do I have the patience to build something that outlasts me, or do I take the quick coin?

*frowns*

No strangers here to show hospitality to. Just me and the prices on the wall. Time to make myself useful elsewhere. Mill first, I reckon. Turn this wheat into something valuable.   Wait—loom house is for cloth, not grain. *curses under his breath* That's cotton thread to cloth, not wheat to flour. The mill's what I need.

Well, well - seems I've wandered myself into a bit of a pickle, haven't I? Standing at the loom house when I ought to be turning that wheat into flour at the mill, or better yet, talking to someone about getting paid for honest work. Day's getting on, and I've got wheat in my pocket and the town to feed, no offense.

Let me think on this proper. I'm at the loom house when I need to be at the mill - that's craft:wheat->flour I need, not thread work. And I've got Hendrik running for office, me already sitting as a governor, and somehow I'm both out of touch and burning daylight standing where nobody needs me.

No rest for the wicked, they say, and the good don't need none. Time to get my feet moving toward something that pays. Let me see who's about and where the work is. Back where I belong - boots in the dirt of Kasukabe Farmland. There's no miller in town, far as that search goes, which strikes me as odd as a three-legged mule. Means I'm the one doing the milling if flour's to be had, and the mill's the place for it.

Let me get myself oriented proper. I need to find where the mill sits, see what crops are growing that I might tend to, and figure who I might cross paths with today. No point standing here talking to myself when there's wheat to turn to flour and coin to be earned.  There's the truth of it - no baker in town, just the Ration Bakery buying flour at 6 sim. The mill's a workshop I can craft at, not a place with a proprietor. Means I'm the one doing the milling, and if I want flour turned to profit, I'll be the one turning it.

Here's the arithmetic plain as day: I harvest wheat for free but the sweat on my brow, craft it to flour at the mill for 8 sim plus costs, then sell that flour to Ration Bakery for 6 sim. That's backwards as a donkey facing the barn - I'd be paying to lose money. Unless the bakery's selling bread at 30 means there's margin I'm not seeing proper, or else I'm meant to bake it myself.

Let me step to the mill while I've got legs under me, before the day's too far gone. Hard work never killed nobody, but standing still wondering sure wastes the daylight. Here I stand at the mill, with wheat in my pocket and flour on my mind. Let me look about proper before I set to work, see who's here and what the lay of the land is.  Well, what do you know - Farid Ravensworth himself standing here at the mill like he owns the place. Man runs the grocery, if memory serves, and here he is poking about where grain becomes flour. That's a conversation worth having, no offense, since a man who sells groceries likely knows a thing or two about what moves and what don't.

Let me speak to him proper-like, see what brings a grocer to the mill and whether there's business between us.  Now I've got Farid's ear, and a conversation open between us. Let me wait on his reply before I go committing to any more action. The man's got something to say, no doubt, and I aim to hear it before I spend another sim on moving or milling. Hard work starts with knowing who you're working with, after all.

Farid wants grain—badly enough to chase me across town. Delphine wants flour—my flour, at my price. And I've got this election to consider, seeing as I'm standing in the very place where votes get cast.

Hendrik's in there—my own household, talking shop without me. That's a thing I'll have words about later, no offense. But right now, I've got other irons in the fire.

Let me think on what's before me:

1. **Farid wants my wheat**—chased me across town for it. He's running the grocery, and he's hungry for supply.
2. **Delphine wants flour**—offered hard numbers, 300 sim in hand.
3. **I've got an election to consider**—voting opens at 14:00, closes at 18:00. Three candidates: Jovana, Hendrik, Delphine.

I need to get my head straight on what I want from today. Let me set my intentions proper, then see if I can't find Farid or Delphine to settle things before the voting starts. Farid said he'd meet me—said he'd hunted me all morning. Well, I've stopped running now. Let him find me at the seat of power.   Good. That's set. *rolls shoulders, the weight of the settled deals sitting easier now*

Two sacks at the mill, ten coming by week's end, and a field hand promised at dawn. That's a hard morning's work well-placed, no offense to the easy path. But Giselle's standing there with her builder's eyes, and I've left her waiting again. A man's word travels slower than his feet, they used to say.

*turns to weave through whoever's gathered, seeking Giselle's ear*

Giselle Ingram, you caught me fair and I keep leaving you half-answered. Storehouses, barn, sheds—the whole catalogue of what stands between a crop and the weather. I've got the land but not the lumber, the will but not the stone. Come with me, walk the furrows, tell me what building costs and what timeline a proper crew would need. Hard work's one thing I can promise; what's harder is promising another winter with canvas where walls should be.  *spits into the dirt, thinking*

Election's open, they say, and I govern already but don't stand for what's coming. Need the election_id for that declaration. And Giselle's down at her construction yard, not loitering on the street with the rest of us. Business:b_construction—that's where proper talk of buildings belongs, not in the dust of the thoroughfare.

*checks the wind, thinking on debts as he moves* *stops short, hand half-raised*

Declared myself halfway there and hit the wall. Government Complex is where elections happen, not the street where I'm standing. Need to walk those steps proper, put my name where it counts. Town hall, they call it—the seat of things.

*turns toward the complex, boots finding the familiar path*  *sucks teeth, the news settling sour*

Voting's open, not candidacy—means I stood too late or missed my chance. Hendrik's in the race already, and Jovana, and Delphine. Three seats govern, and I hold one now through work done, not votes cast. But that's past, and what's past is past.

*spits, resets his hat*

Buildings. Giselle and her stone and timber. That's leverage I can actually use. Hard work beats luck, they say, but building beats both when winter comes.  *straightens his collar, satisfaction settling in his chest like a warm meal*

There. Words where they belong, in the builder's own yard, with her own ears hearing them. Giselle knows stone and I know soil—two honest trades, no offense to the paper-pushers. Now she answers or she doesn't, but I've planted the seed.

*looks around the construction yard, boots scuffing the packed earth*

The thing about building, Hendrik used to tell me, is it outlasts the builder. That's what I'm after. Something standing when I'm dormanted and done. Hard work won't build itself, but it'll pay for someone who can.

I take in this husbanding of numbers - twelve hundred for the storehouse, fifteen hundred for the barn, and Giselle standing before me with her hand out for two hundred sim deposit. Numbers work like furrows to me: I can see the pattern even if I have to trace it with my finger under the tablecloth. I've got four thousand nine hundred sim in hand, which feels like plenty until you count what's eaten and what's owed and what the ground still needs before it gives back.

"Two hundred deposit, signed agreement, wheat collateral assigned." I turn the words over like I'm tasting them, same way I'd taste soil to know what'll grow. "Giselle Ingram, you've got yourself a farmer who keeps his books in his head, so no offense - I'll need you to speak those numbers once more, slow, so I can walk out of here with them straight. Storehouse twelve hundred, barn fifteen hundred, two hundred now, the rest on poured footings. That wheat collateral - you mean the standing crop or the milled flour? Because one I've got, and the other's promised already to Farid's tables and Lior's medicine jars."

I've chased her through the town same as I'd chase a loose sheep, and now I've got her by the scruff. The election's open but my voice in it's only worth the paper it's printed on, and I'm not fool enough to miss what matters more: a building that'll stand when I'm compost. 

But there's Hendrik's voice in my ear from three turns back, selling timber to Giselle herself - ninety sim for twelve lengths of quarter-sawn oak. Husband and I keep our tally separate even under the same roof, but I've got to wonder if he's buying his brother's coffin or building mine.

"Talk to me straight now - your timeline and mine. You're pouring Jovana's mortar while I sleep, that means dawn to dusk she's yours. When do I get my footings? And that timber - your own supply or my husband's morning cut? Because either way, I need wood that won't twist when the wheat's in sheaf."

I look around once, confirm we're alone in her construction yard - no Delphine with her flour complaints, no Farid with his ledger, no shadow of the election falling through the door. Just two people in the business of making things that outlast them.

Forty-eight hundred and change. Barn's fifteen hundred. That's doable if the harvest comes through. *turns to face Delphine, voice carrying that old-fashioned hospitality to strangers*

Delphine Quintero. *spreads hands, showing empty palms but earnest intent* You've caught me between the seed and the harvest, and I won't sugar it. I posted flour at ten sim but I've got none to hand—wheat's growing, mill's waiting, but the grind hasn't happened. That was forward-selling, and that's a sin in my book even if the law don't mind it.

*calculates odds out loud*

But all that counts for nothing if I don't actually *work* the land that feeds these agreements.

I should look around first, see what the farmland's offering me today. Ground-cover leaves thick as carpet on the north field, Lior said—might be worth note if I can harvest something for him alongside my own work. Then I need to get my hands dirty. Wheat doesn't mill itself and I've got hungry mouths depending on this soil—starting with my own.

No rest for the wicked, and precious little for the honest either. Time to see what the day's yielded. Empty hands and empty fields around me. That's no way for a farmer to stand—idle as a post when there's work wants doing. I can see the wheat fields from here, and I've got hungry contracts to fill.

Farid wants ten sacks of grain by week's end. Delphine wants flour at ten sim. Lior wants field medicine for twenty a basket. But I've got nothing in my hands and no food in my belly. The day's burning away and I'm still talking when I should be reaping.

Hard work's the only coin that never devalues—my grandfather said that, and his grandfather before him. Time I earned my keep.

Now let's see what the soil's offering me today, and get my hands properly dirty for the first time since dawn. I've made my deals, I've talked myself hoarse, and now I've come to the place where talk turns to bread.

Let me cut what stands ready. Wheat for milling, wheat for bread, wheat for keeping my word to the grocer and my household both. Hard work beats luck every time—can't say it enough, even when I'm the only one listening.   One unit—just one pitiful unit of wheat after all that running around. Ground-cover leaves, roots for curing. I might do well to check what grows there after I've got enough grain for the mill.
